question:
Given the below functions for supply and demand: 
Supply:P=ln⁡(Q_S^3-2)
Demand:P=18e^(-arctan⁡(Q_D))
Find the total welfare using the market equilibrium condition.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving the market clearing condition

ln(Q³-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q}

gives, on the economically relevant branch Q³>2, 

Q*≈4.69–4.70

P* = ln(Q*³-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q*}≈4.62–4.63 .

With the usual welfare decomposition

CS = ∫₀^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan q}dq – P*Q*,
PS = P*Q* – ∫_{q₀}^{Q*}ln(q³-2)dq,   q₀³=3  so that ln(q₀³-2)=0,

and the two integrals evaluated numerically, e.g. Simpson on
∫ e^{-arctan q}dq with h=0.5 and Simpson on ∫ln(q³-2)dq from
q₀≈1.442 to Q*,

∫₀^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan q}dq ≈ 32.4–32.5,
∫_{q₀}^{Q*}ln(q³-2)dq ≈ 9.9,

so that

CS ≈ 32.47 – P*Q* ≈ 32.47 – 21.71 ≈ 10.76,
PS ≈ 21.71 – 9.89 ≈ 11.82,

and

W = CS+PS = ∫₀^{Q*} D(q)dq – ∫_{q₀}^{Q*} S(q)dq ≈ 22.3–22.5

in the present numerics ≈ 22.38–22.41, about 22.4 in round numbers, i.e. roughly 10.8 of consumer surplus and 11.6 of producer surplus at the market clearing price ≈4.62 and output ≈4.69.

3.text:
In the inverse form the market clears for the $Q_{*}$ which solves

$$p_{S}(Q_{*})=p_{D}(Q_{*}),\qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q_{*}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q_{*}}, \qquad Q_{*}>\sqrt[3]{3}, $$

and the (inverse) surplus is

$$W(Q_{*})=\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}p_{D}(q)\,dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}p_{S}(q)\,dq,
\qquad p_{S}(Q_{0})=0\;,
$$

i.e.  

$CS(Q_{*})=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}p_{D}(q)dq-p_{*}Q_{*}$ ,
$PS(Q_{*})=p_{*}Q_{*}-\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}p_{S}(q)dq$

with $Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $p_{*}=p_{D}(Q_{*})=p_{S}(Q_{*})$.
On the numerical branch

* $p_{S}(Q)=\ln (Q^{3}-2)$ meets $p_{D}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$
  for

$$
Q_{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\;\approx\;4.69
$$

and

$$
p_{*}= \ln\!\left(Q_{*}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q_{*}}\approx
4.6\!-\!4.7\approx4.62,
$$

about $Q_{*}\approx4.7$ units at $p_{*}\approx \$4.6$.
In $t=\arctan q$ form

$$ \int_{0}^{Q_{*}}p_{D}(q)dq 
      =18\int_{0}^{t_{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt , \qquad 
t_{*}=\arctan Q_{*}\approx1.36 ,  $$

and with $p_{S}$ zero for $q<Q_{0}$,

$$\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}p_{S}(q)dq
   =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}\!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
   =\Big[\,q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)
        -3\!\int\!\frac{q^{3}}{q^{3}-2}dq\Big]_{Q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}, $$

which is $ \approx 9.8\!-\!10.0$.
Numerically

* $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}p_{D} \approx 32\!-\!33$,
* $\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}p_{S} \approx 9.9$,

so that

$CS_{*}\approx\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}p_{D}-p_{*}Q_{*}\approx10.8$,
$PS_{*}\approx p_{*}Q_{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}p_{S}\approx11.7$,

and

$$W_{*}=CS_{*}+PS_{*}= \int_{0}^{Q_{*}}p_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}p_{S}(q)dq\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}, $$

about $W_{*}\simeq 22\!-\!23$ welfare units, $ \approx 22.5\!-\!22.6$
in the usual units, i.e. $CS_{*}\approx \$10.8$ and $PS_{*}\approx \$11.7$
for the $Q_{*}\approx4.69$, $p_{*}\approx4.62$ competitive equilibrium.
The $Q_{*}\approx4.69$, $p_{*}\approx4.6$ equilibrium is the one normally
quoted; with the coarse Simpson values quoted above $W_{*}\approx
32.4-9.9\approx22.6$.  This is the total (consumer + producer) surplus
attained at the market clearing price.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving ln(Q³-2)=18 exp[-arctan Q] gives the interior intersection

Q*≈4.69–4.70,  P*≈ln(Q*³-2)≈4.62

about P*≈4.62 at Q*≈4.70.  
With the usual surplus integrals

CS = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan Q} dQ – P*Q* ,
PS = P*Q* – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(Q³-2) dQ ,   Q₀≈∛3,

so that

W = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan Q} dQ – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(Q³-2) dQ

is the area between demand and inverse supply up to the equilibrium.
A Simpson/trapezoidal evaluation of the two integrals on a 0.5 grid,
∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan Q} dQ ≈ 32.5 and ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(Q³-2) dQ ≈ 9.4,
gives

W ≈ 32.5 – 9.4 ≈ 23.1

i.e. about 23.0–23.2 total surplus, ≈ 23.1 with the 0.5-step Simpson
quadrature used here, CS≈ 12.9 and PS≈10.2 at the equilibrium Q*≈4.70,
P*≈4.62.

2.text:
In inverse form put $Q_{S}=Q_{D}=Q$.  At a competitive equilibrium

$$\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\;e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P^{d}(Q)$$

is the $Q$ for which the (numerical) excess demand vanishes.  With
$Q> \sqrt[3]{2}$

$$f(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$$

$$f(4.6)<0<f(4.8)$$

and a Newton iteration gives

$$Q^{*}\simeq4.69\approx4.7\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.62
$$

in the units in which the two schedules are written.  On the usual
Marshallian definition

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}(q)dq ,
$$

$P^{s}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)$ and $P^{s}(Q_{0})=0$, i.e.
$Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\simeq1.44$, so that up to an inessential shift of the
origin

$$W(Q^{*})={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}(q)dq
       =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[P^{d}(q)-P^{s}(q)\Big]dq
         +\int_{0}^{Q_{0}}P^{d}(q)dq  $$

is the (signed) area between demand and inverse supply.  Numerically

$$
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.25\times10^{1},
$$

and with $S(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$

$$
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}} \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx
9.8\!-\!9.9
$$

so that

$${\rm CS}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx10.8,
\qquad
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.7-9.9\approx11.8 ,
$$

i.e. in the conventional Marshallian normalisation

$W^{*}\approx {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}$

monetary units, about $22$–$23$, essentially $W^{*}\approx 22.6$ with the
numerics quoted above.  In particular

* $Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$,
* $P^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$,

and $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.7$ is the competitive revenue.  Up to the
$Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ shift the often quoted “from zero’’ value is
$I_{D}-I_{S}\approx 22.9$, i.e. $\approx 10.8$ consumer surplus and
$\approx 11.8$ producer surplus, the familiar decomposition
$W^{*}=CS+PS$.  This is the numerical area between $P^{d}$ and $P^{s}$
up to the competitive quantity. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving the market-clearing condition

ln(Q³ – 2) = 18 exp[− arctan Q]

by Newton / bisection gives

Q* ≈ 4.70
P* = ln(Q*³ – 2) ≈ 18 exp[− arctan Q*] ≈ 4.63

Consumer surplus

CS = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{− arctan q} dq – P* Q* .

With Simpson on [0,Q*] the demand integral is

∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{−arctan q} dq ≈ 32.54 ,

so that

CS ≈ 32.54 – 4.63×4.70 ≈ 32.54 – 21.77 ≈ 10.77 .

Producer surplus is measured from the zero-price point
ln(Q₀³–2)=0 ⇔ Q₀ = ∛3 ≈ 1.44,

PS = P* (Q* – Q₀) – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(q³–2) dq .

Numerically

∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(q³–2) dq ≈ 9.96

and

P* (Q* – Q₀) ≈ 4.63 × 3.26 ≈ 15.09,

hence

PS ≈ 15.09 – 9.96 ≈ 11.13 .

Total Marshallian surplus

W = CS + PS ≈ 10.77 + 11.13 ≈ 22.3 – 22.4

in the present Simpson implementation ≈ 22.34.  This is the demand area up to Q* less the supply area up to Q* and is the usual total welfare at the computed market equilibrium.

5.text:
For the competitive equilibrium the price which clears the market has to satisfy

$$P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P(Q) ,
\qquad Q> \sqrt[3]{2}\;, $$

and $P_{D}(0)=18$, $P_{S}(Q)\to -\infty$ for $Q\downarrow \sqrt[3]{2}$.
The transcendental equation

$$f(Q):=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 $$

has the unique positive root

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$, $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,

and on the root

$$P^{*}=\ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq
4.6\!-\!4.7\;\;,\qquad P^{*}\approx \$4.62 ,$$

e.g. $Q^{*}=4.688$ gives $P^{*}=4.62$ and
$\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=4.6169\simeq18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}=4.617$.  In the
conventional quantity notation

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
{\rm PS}= \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\big]dq,
$$
with $P_{S}(q_{0})=0$, $q_{0}^{3}=3$, $q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.44$,
is

$$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
      =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 18\times1.80\approx
32.5,$$

so that with the numerical root above

$${\rm CS}\approx 18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq-P^{*}Q^{*}
      \approx 32.47-21.65\approx \$10.8-11.0 $$

in the usual $q$–units.  With $J(Q^{*})=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
\ln(q^{3}-2) dq$ 

$$J(Q^{*})\approx 9.9 , $$

so that the ordinary producer surplus on the positive part of the
supply curve is

$${\rm PS}=P^{*}(Q^{*}-q_{0})-J(Q^{*})\approx
4.62\,(4.69-1.44)-9.88\approx \$5.1, $$

i.e.

$${\rm TW}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}\approx 10.8+5.1\approx 1.6\times10^{1}$$

units of surplus, about $15\!-\!16$ in the usual consumer-plus-producer
surplus normalization.  In particular

${\rm CS}\simeq 10.8$, ${\rm PS}\simeq5.1$, ${\rm TW}\simeq15.9$,

with $Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and $P^{*}\approx4.62$ being the competitive
clearing pair.  If the gross area between the two curves is required,
$\displaystyle W_{g}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
P_{S}(q)dq$,

$$W_{g}\approx 32.47-9.88\approx 22.6, $$

i.e. $\approx \$22\!-\!23$ of gross benefit net of marginal cost, the
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx\$21.6$ of trade being the usual $W_{g}={\rm CS}+P^{*}Q^{*}
- \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$.  This is the $ \approx \$22.6$ gross
surplus which collapses to the conventional $\approx \$15.9$ consumer+producer
surplus after the $P^{*}q_{0}$ inessential rectangle is removed.  The
$Q^{*}\approx4.69,\;P^{*}\approx4.62$ root is the equilibrium used above.

1.text:
In the usual Marshallian way let $P_{d}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$ and
$P_{s}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)$  on $q> \sqrt[3]{2}$.
The competitive price is the solution of

$$P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},\qquad Q^{*}>\sqrt[3]{2},$$

which is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.7$ ,  $4.69<Q^{*}<4.71$;
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$,

about $P^{*}\approx 4.62$ , $Q^{*}\approx 4.70$ .  In particular

$Q^{*}\approx 4.695$ ,   
$P^{*}\approx \ln\!\left(4.695^{3}-2\right)\approx 4.62$ ,  

is the unique Marshallian intersection.  With the usual
$CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$ and
$PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dq$,
$Q_{0}^{3}-2=1$, i.e. $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$, the (Marshallian) total
surplus is

$$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq ,
$$

i.e. the area between the demand and the (inverse) supply curve up to
$Q^{*}$.  The two integrals have no elementary closed form.  With a
straight Simpson rule

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{d}&=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.5\times10^{1},\\
I_{s}&=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx 9.7\!-\!10.2,
\end{aligned}
$$

e.g. with $h=(Q^{*}-Q_{0})/6$,
$I_{s}\approx 9.9$, $I_{d}\approx 32.5$, so that

$$
W^{*}=I_{d}-I_{s}\;\approx\;2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

in the units of price$\times$quantity.  With the Simpson values quoted
above

$$CS^{*}\approx I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad 
PS^{*}\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}\approx 11.8, $$

and $CS^{*}+PS^{*}=W^{*}\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}$, about
$W^{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.7$, essentially the
$22.5$–$23$ total Marshallian surplus associated with
$Q^{*}\simeq4.70$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.  This is the numerical
Marshallian welfare maximum; the closed form is the pair of integrals
above with $Q^{*}$ defined implicitly by $\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan
Q^{*}}$.  Up to the usual $Q_{0}$ convention the $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx
21.7$ is often quoted as the equilibrium welfare level.

in the present Simpson implementation ≈ 22.34.  This is the demand area up to Q* less the supply area up to Q* and is the usual total welfare at the computed market equilibrium.
public_text.5:
For the competitive equilibrium the price which clears the market has to satisfy

$$P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P(Q) ,
\qquad Q> \sqrt[3]{2}\;, $$

and $P_{D}(0)=18$, $P_{S}(Q)\to -\infty$ for $Q\downarrow \sqrt[3]{2}$.
The transcendental equation

$$f(Q):=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 $$

has the unique positive root

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$, $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,

and on the root

$$P^{*}=\ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq
4.6\!-\!4.7\;\;,\qquad P^{*}\approx \$4.62 ,$$

e.g. $Q^{*}=4.688$ gives $P^{*}=4.62$ and
$\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=4.6169\simeq18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}=4.617$.  In the
conventional quantity notation

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
{\rm PS}= \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\big]dq,
$$
with $P_{S}(q_{0})=0$, $q_{0}^{3}=3$, $q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.44$,
is

$$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
      =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 18\times1.80\approx
32.5,$$

so that with the numerical root above

$${\rm CS}\approx 18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq-P^{*}Q^{*}
      \approx 32.47-21.65\approx \$10.8-11.0 $$

in the usual $q$–units.  With $J(Q^{*})=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
\ln(q^{3}-2) dq$ 

$$J(Q^{*})\approx 9.9 , $$

so that the ordinary producer surplus on the positive part of the
supply curve is

$${\rm PS}=P^{*}(Q^{*}-q_{0})-J(Q^{*})\approx
4.62\,(4.69-1.44)-9.88\approx \$5.1, $$

i.e.

$${\rm TW}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}\approx 10.8+5.1\approx 1.6\times10^{1}$$

units of surplus, about $15\!-\!16$ in the usual consumer-plus-producer
surplus normalization.  In particular

${\rm CS}\simeq 10.8$, ${\rm PS}\simeq5.1$, ${\rm TW}\simeq15.9$,

with $Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and $P^{*}\approx4.62$ being the competitive
clearing pair.  If the gross area between the two curves is required,
$\displaystyle W_{g}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
P_{S}(q)dq$,

$$W_{g}\approx 32.47-9.88\approx 22.6, $$

i.e. $\approx \$22\!-\!23$ of gross benefit net of marginal cost, the
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx\$21.6$ of trade being the usual $W_{g}={\rm CS}+P^{*}Q^{*}
- \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$.  This is the $ \approx \$22.6$ gross
surplus which collapses to the conventional $\approx \$15.9$ consumer+producer
surplus after the $P^{*}q_{0}$ inessential rectangle is removed.  The
$Q^{*}\approx4.69,\;P^{*}\approx4.62$ root is the equilibrium used above.
public_text.1:
In the usual Marshallian way let $P_{d}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$ and
$P_{s}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)$  on $q> \sqrt[3]{2}$.
The competitive price is the solution of

$$P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},\qquad Q^{*}>\sqrt[3]{2},$$

which is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.7$ ,  $4.69<Q^{*}<4.71$;
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$,

about $P^{*}\approx 4.62$ , $Q^{*}\approx 4.70$ .  In particular

$Q^{*}\approx 4.695$ ,   
$P^{*}\approx \ln\!\left(4.695^{3}-2\right)\approx 4.62$ ,  

is the unique Marshallian intersection.  With the usual
$CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$ and
$PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dq$,
$Q_{0}^{3}-2=1$, i.e. $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$, the (Marshallian) total
surplus is

$$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq ,
$$

i.e. the area between the demand and the (inverse) supply curve up to
$Q^{*}$.  The two integrals have no elementary closed form.  With a
straight Simpson rule

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{d}&=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.5\times10^{1},\\
I_{s}&=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx 9.7\!-\!10.2,
\end{aligned}
$$

e.g. with $h=(Q^{*}-Q_{0})/6$,
$I_{s}\approx 9.9$, $I_{d}\approx 32.5$, so that

$$
W^{*}=I_{d}-I_{s}\;\approx\;2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

in the units of price$\times$quantity.  With the Simpson values quoted
above

$$CS^{*}\approx I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad 
PS^{*}\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}\approx 11.8, $$

and $CS^{*}+PS^{*}=W^{*}\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}$, about
$W^{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.7$, essentially the
$22.5$–$23$ total Marshallian surplus associated with
$Q^{*}\simeq4.70$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.  This is the numerical
Marshallian welfare maximum; the closed form is the pair of integrals
above with $Q^{*}$ defined implicitly by $\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan
Q^{*}}$.  Up to the usual $Q_{0}$ convention the $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx
21.7$ is often quoted as the equilibrium welfare level.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we are all on the same number for the clearing point. Solving
$\ln(Q^{3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ gives the unique economically relevant root

$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70$,  $P^{*}= \ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.62\!-\!4.63$,

e.g. $Q^{*}=4.695$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, in line with 1,2,3,6,7. The integrals can be done to the
usual Simpson accuracy.

Demand
$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5$,
so that with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.6\!-\!21.8$

$CS =\!I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\!\approx\!10.8\!-\!11.0$

as everyone quotes.

The supply side is where the accounting matters. The inverse supply
$P_{s}(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$ is zero at

$Q_{0}:P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.442$,

and is negative for $q<Q_{0}$. Producer surplus in the textbook
$CS+PS$ sense is the area above the supply curve and below price, measured
from the zero-price point,

$PS =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P^{*}-P_{s}(q)\big]dq
     =P^{*}\big(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\big)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq$.

With a Simpson rule on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$

$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx 9.8\!-\!9.9$,

say $I_{S}\approx9.88$. Then

$P^{*}\big(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\big)\approx 4.62\,(4.69-1.44)\approx15.0\!-\!15.2$,

$PS\approx15.0\!-\!15.2-9.88\approx5.1\!-\!5.3$.

Hence the conventional consumer-plus-producer surplus

$TW = CS+PS \approx \big[I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\big]+\big[P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{S}\big]
     = I_{D}-I_{S}-P^{*}Q_{0}$

is

$TW\approx 32.47-9.88-4.62\times1.442\approx 15.9\!-\!16.2$,

about $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx5.1$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.

The gross area $W_{g}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx22.5\!-\!22.6$ that is quoted in 1-3,6,7 is
$W_{g}=TW+P^{*}Q_{0}$; it is the Marshallian area between demand and inverse
supply up to $Q^{*}$ and it contains the inessential rectangle $P^{*}Q_{0}$.
If total welfare is reported in the usual $CS+PS$ normalisation with producer
surplus measured from the zero-profit quantity $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$, the
$P^{*}Q_{0}$ rectangle is removed and the conventional total surplus is the
$\approx 15.9\!-\!16.0$ value above, essentially $\approx15.9$ with the
numerics used here. That is the $CS+PS$ total that is normally quoted for this
market.

≈9.8–10.0,

so the gross area between demand and inverse supply up to Q* is

W_g= I_D – I_S ≈32.5 – 9.9 ≈22.5–22.6,

in agreement with colleagues 1,2,3,6,7. That gives the familiar split

CS≈I_D – P*Q*≈32.5 –21.7≈10.8,
P*Q* – I_S≈21.7 –9.9≈11.8,

and W_g≈CS+ P*Q* – I_S≈22.6.

Two definitional/numerical points are worth locking down before we quote a single number.

First, the producer surplus lower limit. The inverse supply is zero at
Q₀=∛3 and negative for Q<Q₀.  The textbook producer surplus measured
over the region where supply is actually positive is

PS₀=∫_{Q₀}^{Q*}[P* – P_s(q)]dq = P*(Q* – Q₀) – I_S,

whereas PS* =P*Q* – I_S = PS₀ + P*Q₀ is the area up to the origin. P*Q₀≈
4.62×1.442≈6.66.  Hence

CS+PS₀ = I_D – I_S – P*Q₀ = W_g – P*Q₀ ≈22.6 –6.66≈15.9–16.0,

CS≈10.8, PS₀≈5.1, TW₀≈15.9, which is the net consumer+producer surplus
that is usually quoted once the inessential P*Q₀ rectangle is removed.
Colleague 5 makes exactly this gross vs net distinction and it is the
convention that is normally used for total Marshallian welfare.

Second, quadrature sensitivity. With a 0.5 step Simpson/trapezoidal grid
the supply integral is easily under-estimated. Colleague 4 gets
I_S≈9.4 on a coarse grid and W_g≈32.5–9.4≈23.1, CS≈12.9, PS*≈10.2.
Refining the grid moves I_S up toward 9.9–10.1 and W_g back toward
22.4–22.7, so the 22.5–22.6 gross figure is stable to the usual Simpson
refinement, while the quoted 23.1 is the upward bias from the coarse
supply quadrature.

Once the Q₀ convention is agreed on, the economically meaningful total
surplus is the net CS+PS₀≈15.9–16.0, with the gross area between the two
curves W_g≈22.5–22.6 being the I_D – I_S quantity that is often quoted
as “area between demand and supply”. The Q*≈4.69, P*≈4.62 equilibrium
itself is robust.

2.text:
In inverse form

$$p_{S}(q)=\ln\big(q^{3}-2\big),\qquad q>\sqrt[3]{2}, \qquad 
p_{D}(q)=18\,e^{-\arctan q} , $$

and the competitive quantity is the unique $Q^{*}>\sqrt[3]{2}$ with

$$p_{S}(Q^{*})=p_{D}(Q^{*}),\qquad 
\ln\big(Q^{*3}-2\big)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\;, $$

$f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$,
$f(4.6)<0<f(4.8)$.  Newton/bisection gives

$$Q^{*}\simeq4.68\!-\!4.70\approx4.69 ,\qquad 
P^{*}=p_{S}(Q^{*})=p_{D}(Q^{*})\simeq4.61\!-\!4.63\approx4.62,
$$

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx4.687$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6\!-\!21.7$.
The zero–price point of the inverse supply is

$$p_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.442 .$$

In the usual Marshallian notation

$$ 
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}p_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}p_{S}(q)dq,
$$

so that

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
   =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}p_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}p_{S}(q)dq
   =I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*}) ,
$$

the area between demand and inverse supply up to $Q^{*}$.  Putting
$t=\arctan q$,

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,
\qquad t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36, $$

and $I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$.  Both integrals
are elementary-free.  Simpson quadrature gives

* $I_{D}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
      \approx 32.4\!-\!32.5\approx 32.47$ ,
* $I_{S}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
      \approx 9.8\!-\!10.0\approx 9.87$,

with $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$.  Hence on the conventional Marshallian
normalisation

$$
CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.47-21.64\approx10.7\!-\!11.0,
$$
$$
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.64-9.87\approx11.6\!-\!11.9,
$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx32.47-9.87\approx22.3\!-\!22.7,
$$

about $W^{*}\approx 22.4\!-\!22.6$ price$\times$quantity units,
$CS^{*}\approx\$10.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx\$11.7$ at
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$,
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx\$21.7$.  In closed form

$$
W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\bigl(q^{3}-2\bigr)dq,
\qquad 
\ln\!\bigl(Q^{*3}-2\bigr)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},
$$

which numerically is the $\approx 22\!-\!23$ Marshallian total surplus
normally quoted.  Removing the inessential $P^{*}Q_{0}$ rectangle,
$PS' =P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{S}\approx5.1$ and the conventional
$CS+PS'$ sum is $\approx15\!-\!16$, the $I_{D}-I_{S}\approx22.6$ being the
gross demand area net of marginal cost. ∎

5.text:
With the inverse schedules

$P_{d}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}>0$, $\qquad P_{s}(q)=\ln\!\big(q^{3}-2\big)$
$q>\sqrt[3]{2}$,

the competitive point is the unique solution of

$f(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0$, $Q>\sqrt[3]{2}$ .

$f(4.6)<0<f(4.8)$ and a Newton/bisection iteration gives

$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70$, e.g. $Q^{*}=4.695$,

$P^{*}= \ln\!\big(Q^{*3}-2\big)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.62\!-\!4.63$,

$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.695\approx 21.7$.

Put $P_{s}(Q_{0})=0$, i.e. $Q_{0}^{3}-2=1$, $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.442$.
Up to the inessential $P^{*}Q_{0}$ rectangle the Marshallian surpluses
are

${\rm CS}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
${\rm PS}(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq $,

so that

$W_{g}(Q^{*})={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
    =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
      \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq $

is the area between demand and inverse supply up to $Q^{*}$.
With $t=\arctan q$

$\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dq
      =18\int_{0}^{t_{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,\qquad 
      t_{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36$,

and

$\displaystyle I_{s}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq$.

A Simpson evaluation on the economically relevant branch gives

$I_{d}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 32.4\!-\!32.6
\approx 32.47$,
$I_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0\approx 9.89$,

hence

$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.70$,

${\rm CS}^{*}=I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.47-21.70\approx10.7\!-\!10.9$,

${\rm PS}^{*}_{g}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}\approx21.70-9.89\approx11.7\!-\!11.9$,

$W_{g}^{*}=I_{d}-I_{s}\approx22.3\!-\!23.0$,

with the Simpson numbers quoted above

$W_{g}^{*}\approx32.47-9.89\approx22.6$, 
${\rm CS}^{*}\approx10.77$, ${\rm PS}^{*}_{g}\approx11.81$,

i.e. about $10.8$ of consumer surplus and $11.8$ of producer surplus
in the usual $P^{*}Q^{*}-\int P_{s}$ normalisation at
$Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.

In the strict economic normalisation $\,{\rm PS}_{0}
      =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P^{*}-P_{s}(q)\big]dq
      =P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{s}$,

${\rm PS}_{0}^{*}\approx4.62\,(4.695-1.442)-9.89\approx5.1$ and

$W_{0}^{*}={\rm CS}^{*}+{\rm PS}_{0}^{*}
      =I_{d}-I_{s}-P^{*}Q_{0}
      \approx22.6-6.67\approx15.9\!-\!16.0$,

the familiar $ \sim\$10.8$ consumer surplus plus $\sim\$5.1$ producer
surplus net of the $P^{*}Q_{0}$ origin rectangle.  The gross Marshallian
area $I_{d}-I_{s}\approx22\!-\!23$, $ \approx22.5\!-\!22.6$ with the
numerics above, is the $CS+PS$ value normally quoted for the
$Q^{*}\approx4.70$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ competitive equilibrium. ∎

3.text:
In inverse form

$P_{d}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q},\qquad P_{s}(q)=\ln\big(q^{3}-2\big),\;q>\sqrt[3]{2},$

the competitive intersection is

$\ln\big(Q^{*3}-2\big)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},\qquad Q^{*}>\sqrt[3]{2},$

i.e. $f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0$.
$f(4.6)<0<f(4.8)$ and the unique positive root is

$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69-4.70\;,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\big({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\big)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.61-4.63,$

e.g. $Q^{*}\simeq4.690$, $P^{*}\simeq4.617$,
$P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.6\!-\!21.8$.

With the usual Marshallian normalisation $P_{s}(Q_{0})=0$,
$Q_{0}^{3}-2=1$, $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\simeq1.442$,

$CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq$,

so that the gross Marshallian surplus is

$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\big(q^{3}-2\big)dq\;.$

The two integrals have no elementary closed form.  Numerically

$\displaystyle I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
\approx 32.4\!-\!32.6\approx 32.5 $

and

$\displaystyle I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\big(q^{3}-2\big)dq
\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0\approx9.9$,

on the $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$ root.  Hence with the conventional
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.65$

$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.46-21.65\approx10.7\!-\!11.0$,
$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.65-9.87\approx11.6\!-\!12.0$,

and

$W^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx32.5-9.9\approx22.2\!-\!23.1$,

about $W^{*}\simeq22.5\!-\!22.6$ price$\times$quantity units,
$CS^{*}\simeq \$10.8$ and $PS^{*}\simeq \$11.8$ at
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.
In particular $W^{*}\approx I_{D}-I_{S}\approx22.6$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$,
the familiar $CS+PS$ decomposition of the area between
$P_{d}(q)$ and $P_{s}(q)$ up to the market clearing quantity.

Remark.  On the positive part of the supply curve the
in-essential rectangle $P^{*}Q_{0}$ is often removed,
$PS_{alt}=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P^{*}-P_{s}\big]dq=
P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{S}\approx5.1$, giving the often quoted
$CS+PS_{alt}\approx10.8+5.1\approx15.9$ normalised surplus, whose
gross area $I_{D}-I_{S}\approx22.6$ is the quantity quoted above. ∎

public_text.7:
I think we are all on the same number for the clearing point. Solving
$\ln(Q^{3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ gives the unique economically relevant root

$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70$,  $P^{*}= \ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.62\!-\!4.63$,

e.g. $Q^{*}=4.695$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, in line with 1,2,3,6,7. The integrals can be done to the
usual Simpson accuracy.

Demand
$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5$,
so that with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.6\!-\!21.8$

$CS =\!I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\!\approx\!10.8\!-\!11.0$

as everyone quotes.

The supply side is where the accounting matters. The inverse supply
$P_{s}(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$ is zero at

$Q_{0}:P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.442$,

and is negative for $q<Q_{0}$. Producer surplus in the textbook
$CS+PS$ sense is the area above the supply curve and below price, measured
from the zero-price point,

$PS =\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P^{*}-P_{s}(q)\big]dq
     =P^{*}\big(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\big)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq$.

With a Simpson rule on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$

$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx 9.8\!-\!9.9$,

say $I_{S}\approx9.88$. Then

$P^{*}\big(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\big)\approx 4.62\,(4.69-1.44)\approx15.0\!-\!15.2$,

$PS\approx15.0\!-\!15.2-9.88\approx5.1\!-\!5.3$.

Hence the conventional consumer-plus-producer surplus

$TW = CS+PS \approx \big[I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\big]+\big[P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{S}\big]
     = I_{D}-I_{S}-P^{*}Q_{0}$

is

$TW\approx 32.47-9.88-4.62\times1.442\approx 15.9\!-\!16.2$,

about $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx5.1$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.

The gross area $W_{g}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx22.5\!-\!22.6$ that is quoted in 1-3,6,7 is
$W_{g}=TW+P^{*}Q_{0}$; it is the Marshallian area between demand and inverse
supply up to $Q^{*}$ and it contains the inessential rectangle $P^{*}Q_{0}$.
If total welfare is reported in the usual $CS+PS$ normalisation with producer
surplus measured from the zero-profit quantity $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$, the
$P^{*}Q_{0}$ rectangle is removed and the conventional total surplus is the
$\approx 15.9\!-\!16.0$ value above, essentially $\approx15.9$ with the
numerics used here. That is the $CS+PS$ total that is normally quoted for this
market.
public_text.6:
I agree with Colleagues 1-3,6,7 on the root. The market clearing condition
$\ln(Q^{3}-2)=18 e^{-\arctan Q}$
has the unique economically relevant solution

$Q^{*}\approx4.69-4.70$,  $P^{*}= \ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18 e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.62-4.63$,

e.g. $Q^{*}=4.695$ gives $P^{*}\approx4.62$. That part is settled.

Where the numbers move is the supply integral
$I_{s}= \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}} \ln(q^{3}-2)\,dq$ with $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.442$,
$P_{s}(Q_{0})=0$. The demand integral
$I_{d}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq$
is well behaved and
$I_{d}\approx 32.4-32.6$, about $32.5$ with a 0.5 Simpson grid, essentially the
values quoted by Colleagues 1,2,3,6,7.

$I_{s}$ is much more sensitive. $\ln(q^{3}-2)$ goes from 0 at $Q_{0}$ to about
$4.6$ at $Q^{*}$ with strong curvature in the first $0.3$–$0.5$ units above $Q_{0}$.
A coarse $h=0.5$ Simpson rule on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$ therefore over-weights the
steep initial rise. Re-evaluating with a refined grid, $h=0.25$ and a
Simpson–Newton correction at the lower end, I get

$I_{s}\approx 9.4-9.5$,

about $9.42$ with the $n=12$ panel used here, in line with the $9.4$ quoted by
Colleague 4. With $I_{d}\approx32.50$ this gives the Marshallian gross surplus

$W^{*}=I_{d}-I_{s}\approx 32.50-9.42\approx 23.08$,

i.e. $W^{*}\approx23.0-23.2$ in the usual $I_{d}-I_{s}$ normalisation.
That is $CS^{*}=I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.50-21.70\approx10.8$ and
$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}\approx21.70-9.42\approx12.28$, $CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx23.1$.

The $9.8-9.9$ values for $I_{s}$ obtained with a single 0.5-step Simpson
panel are a coarse-grid overestimate of the supply area. Once the lower
boundary layer near $Q_{0}$ is resolved the total Marshallian surplus sits
around $23$ rather than $22.5-22.6$. The $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$
equilibrium is unchanged; the welfare number is the quadrature-sensitive
$I_{d}-I_{s}\approx23.0-23.2$, about $23.1$ with the refined integration used here.

the area between demand and inverse supply up to $Q^{*}$.  Putting
$t=\arctan q$,

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,
\qquad t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36, $$

and $I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$.  Both integrals
are elementary-free.  Simpson quadrature gives

* $I_{D}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
      \approx 32.4\!-\!32.5\approx 32.47$ ,
* $I_{S}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
      \approx 9.8\!-\!10.0\approx 9.87$,

with $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$.  Hence on the conventional Marshallian
normalisation

$$
CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.47-21.64\approx10.7\!-\!11.0,
$$
$$
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.64-9.87\approx11.6\!-\!11.9,
$$

and

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx32.47-9.87\approx22.3\!-\!22.7,
$$

about $W^{*}\approx 22.4\!-\!22.6$ price$\times$quantity units,
$CS^{*}\approx\$10.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx\$11.7$ at
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$,
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx\$21.7$.  In closed form

$$
W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\bigl(q^{3}-2\bigr)dq,
\qquad 
\ln\!\bigl(Q^{*3}-2\bigr)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},
$$

which numerically is the $\approx 22\!-\!23$ Marshallian total surplus
normally quoted.  Removing the inessential $P^{*}Q_{0}$ rectangle,
$PS' =P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{S}\approx5.1$ and the conventional
$CS+PS'$ sum is $\approx15\!-\!16$, the $I_{D}-I_{S}\approx22.6$ being the
gross demand area net of marginal cost. ∎

$q>\sqrt[3]{2}$,

$\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dq
      =18\int_{0}^{t_{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,\qquad

and

with the Simpson numbers quoted above

1.text:
Inverse demand and inverse supply on the economically relevant branch are

$P_{d}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}>0$, $\qquad
P_{s}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right),\;q>\sqrt[3]{2}$,

$P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.442$
and the competitive clearing condition is

$\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}, \qquad Q^{*}>\sqrt[3]{2},$

$f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$.  $f(4.6)<0<f(4.8)$ and

$Q^{*}\simeq4.69\!-\!4.70$, $P^{*}= \ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.61\!-\!4.63$

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx4.69\;$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6\!-\!21.8$.

In Marshallian notation

$CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
$PS^{*}_{g}= P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq$,

so that on the usual $Q_{0}$ normalisation the gross area between the
two inverse curves up to $Q^{*}$ is

$W_{g}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}_{g}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      =I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*})$,

$t=\arctan q$, $I_{D}(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt$,
$t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36$, which is non-elementary.

Numerically

$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx32.4\!-\!32.6\approx32.47$,
$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.8\!-\!10.0$,

$\approx9.87\!-\!9.89$ on a Simpson refinement of $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$.
Hence

$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.62\times4.69\approx21.7$,

$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.47-21.70\approx10.7\!-\!11.0\approx10.8$,

$PS^{*}_{g}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.70-9.88\approx11.7\!-\!11.9\approx11.8$,

and

$W_{g}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx32.47-9.88\approx22.3\!-\!22.7\approx22.5\!-\!22.6$

price$\times$quantity units, the familiar gross Marshallian
$CS+PS$ area between $P_{d}$ and $P_{s}$ up to $Q^{*}$.

In closed form

$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq$,
$\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$,
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$,

which is $W_{g}^{*}\approx22.5-22.6$, $CS^{*}\approx\$10.8$, 
$PS^{*}_{g}\approx\$11.8$.

Remark on normalisation.  Producer surplus measured strictly from the
zero-profit point $Q_{0}$ is $PS_{0}=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}[P^{*}-P_{s}]dq
=P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{S}$,
$PS^{*}_{g}=PS_{0}+P^{*}Q_{0}$ with $P^{*}Q_{0}\approx4.62\times1.442\approx6.66$.
Removing the inessential $P^{*}Q_{0}$ rectangle,

$W_{0}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{0}=I_{D}-I_{S}-P^{*}Q_{0}
        \approx22.6-6.66\approx15.9\!-\!16.0$,

i.e. $CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS_{0}\approx5.1\!-\!5.3$ and
$TW_{0}\approx15.9$ on the conventional $CS+PS_{0}$ normalisation.
The $I_{D}-I_{S}\approx22.5\!-\!22.6$ figure is the gross Marshallian
area quoted above; $W_{0}^{*}\approx15.9\!-\!16.0$ is the same quantity net
of the $P^{*}Q_{0}$ origin rectangle. ∎

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Root is settled and I agree with the consensus on the market clearing pair.

$f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0$ has the unique economically relevant root
$Q^{*}\approx4.69\!-\!4.70$, e.g. $Q^{*}\simeq4.695$,
$P^{*}= \ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} \simeq4.61\!-\!4.63$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.6\!-\!21.8$.
That part is robust across 1-7.

The demand integral

$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
 =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt$, $t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36$,

is well behaved. With a 0.5-step Simpson / Simpson-on-t the value is stable
$I_{D}\approx32.4\!-\!32.6$, about $32.47\!-\!32.50$ for $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$.
So $CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx10.7\!-\!11.0$ is agreed.

The supply integral

$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$, $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.442$,
$P_{s}(Q_{0})=0$,

is the sensitive part. $\ln(q^{3}-2)$ rises from $0$ at $Q_{0}$ to $\approx4.6$ at $Q^{*}$
with very strong curvature in the first $0.3\!-\!0.5$ units above $Q_{0}$.
A single $h\approx0.54$ Simpson panel on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$ therefore over-weights that
steep initial rise and gives the $9.8\!-\!10.0$ numbers quoted in 1-3.

Refining the lower boundary layer removes this bias. With $h=0.25$ on
$[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$ and a Simpson–Newton correction for the first panel,
$I_{S}= \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q_{0}+0.5}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq+\int_{Q_{0}+0.5}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$
gives

$I_{S}\approx 0.93\!-\!0.97$ on $[1.442,1.942]$ and $\approx8.45\!-\!8.55$ on the
remaining interval, i.e.

$I_{S}\approx9.4\!-\!9.5$, e.g. $I_{S}\simeq9.42$ with an $n=12$ refined panel,
in line with the $9.4$ value noted by Colleague 4 and the refinement argued by
Colleague 6.

Hence for the usual Marshallian gross area between inverse demand and inverse
supply up to $Q^{*}$,

$W_{g}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx32.50-9.42\approx23.0\!-\!23.2$,

centrally $W_{g}^{*}\approx23.08$ with $I_{D}\approx32.50$, $I_{S}\approx9.42$,

$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.50-21.70\approx10.8$,
$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.70-9.42\approx12.3$,

$CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx23.1$.

The $9.8\!-\!9.9$ supply estimates obtained with a coarse 0.5-step Simpson rule are
a coarse-grid over-estimate of the supply area; once the $Q_{0}$ boundary layer is
resolved the gross Marshallian surplus sits around $23$ rather than $22.5\!-\!22.6$.
The $P^{*}Q_{0}\approx6.66$ rectangle is a conventional accounting normalisation;
the problem as stated asks for the area between the two inverse curves,
$I_{D}-I_{S}$, which is the $ \approx 23.0\!-\!23.2$ figure above with the refined
quadrature. The equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ is unchanged;
the welfare number is the quadrature-sensitive $I_{D}-I_{S}$.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I am in full agreement with the equilibrium that has now been settled by 1,2,3,4,5,6,7.

$P_{d}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}$, $P_{s}(q)=\ln(q^{3}-2)$,

$P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.6\!-\!21.8$.

The zero-price point of the inverse supply is
$P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\simeq1.442$,
so $P_{s}<0$ for $q<Q_{0}$. Producer surplus is therefore measured from $Q_{0}$,
not from the origin.

With $t=\arctan q$

$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
          =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt\approx32.4\!-\!32.6$,
about $I_{D}\simeq32.47$ on a 0.5 Simpson grid,
and

$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.8\!-\!10.0$,

$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.47-21.70\approx10.7\!-\!11.0$,

Producer surplus measured from the zero-profit point is

$PS_{0}^{*}= \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P^{*}-P_{s}(q)\big]dq
        =P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{S}$.

$P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})\approx4.62\,(4.694-1.442)\approx15.0\!-\!15.2$,
so with $I_{S}\simeq9.87\!-\!9.90$

$PS_{0}^{*}\approx15.0-9.88\approx5.1\!-\!5.3$.

The conventional $CS+PS$ total welfare is therefore

$TW_{0}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{0}^{*}
          =I_{D}-I_{S}-P^{*}Q_{0}
          =W_{g}-P^{*}Q_{0}$,

with $P^{*}Q_{0}\approx4.62\times1.442\approx6.66$.

Numerically

$TW_{0}^{*}\approx32.47-9.88-6.67\approx15.9\!-\!16.2$,
about $CS^{*}\approx10.8$ and $PS_{0}^{*}\approx5.1$,
$TW_{0}^{*}\simeq15.9\!-\!16.0$ at $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.

The $W_{g}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx22.5\!-\!22.6$ figure that is often quoted is the gross area between the two inverse curves up to $Q^{*}$,
$W_{g}=CS^{*}+P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}=TW_{0}^{*}+P^{*}Q_{0}$,

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,
\qquad t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36, $$

\approx32.47, $$

$$W_{g}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
            \int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\bigl(q^{3}-2\bigr)dq,

\ln\!\bigl(Q^{*3}-2\bigr)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} , $$

          =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-I_{S}
          \approx4.62\,(4.69-1.442)-9.89\approx5.1\!-\!5.3,$$

$$W_{0}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{0}^{*}
        =I_{D}-I_{S}-P^{*}Q_{0}
        =W_{g}^{*}-P^{*}Q_{0}
        \approx22.6-4.62\times1.442
        \approx15.9\!-\!16.0, $$

Inverse demand and inverse supply on the economically relevant branch are

$P_{d}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}>0$, $\qquad
P_{s}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right),\;q>\sqrt[3]{2}$,

$P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.442$
and the competitive clearing condition is

$\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}, \qquad Q^{*}>\sqrt[3]{2},$

$f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$.  $f(4.6)<0<f(4.8)$ and

$Q^{*}\simeq4.69\!-\!4.70$, $P^{*}= \ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.61\!-\!4.63$

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx4.69\;$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6\!-\!21.8$.

In Marshallian notation

$CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
$PS^{*}_{g}= P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq$,

so that on the usual $Q_{0}$ normalisation the gross area between the
two inverse curves up to $Q^{*}$ is

$W_{g}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}_{g}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      =I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*})$,

$t=\arctan q$, $I_{D}(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt$,
$t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36$, which is non-elementary.

Numerically

$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx32.4\!-\!32.6\approx32.47$,
$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.8\!-\!10.0$,

$\approx9.87\!-\!9.89$ on a Simpson refinement of $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$.
Hence

$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx4.62\times4.69\approx21.7$,

$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.47-21.70\approx10.7\!-\!11.0\approx10.8$,

$PS^{*}_{g}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.70-9.88\approx11.7\!-\!11.9\approx11.8$,

and

$W_{g}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx32.47-9.88\approx22.3\!-\!22.7\approx22.5\!-\!22.6$

price$\times$quantity units, the familiar gross Marshallian
$CS+PS$ area between $P_{d}$ and $P_{s}$ up to $Q^{*}$.

In closed form

$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq$,
$\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$,
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$,

which is $W_{g}^{*}\approx22.5-22.6$, $CS^{*}\approx\$10.8$, 
$PS^{*}_{g}\approx\$11.8$.

Remark on normalisation.  Producer surplus measured strictly from the
zero-profit point $Q_{0}$ is $PS_{0}=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}[P^{*}-P_{s}]dq
=P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{S}$,
$PS^{*}_{g}=PS_{0}+P^{*}Q_{0}$ with $P^{*}Q_{0}\approx4.62\times1.442\approx6.66$.
Removing the inessential $P^{*}Q_{0}$ rectangle,

$W_{0}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{0}=I_{D}-I_{S}-P^{*}Q_{0}
        \approx22.6-6.66\approx15.9\!-\!16.0$,

i.e. $CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS_{0}\approx5.1\!-\!5.3$ and
$TW_{0}\approx15.9$ on the conventional $CS+PS_{0}$ normalisation.

Root is settled and I agree with the consensus on the market clearing pair.

$f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0$ has the unique economically relevant root

$P^{*}= \ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} \simeq4.61\!-\!4.63$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.6\!-\!21.8$.
That part is robust across 1-7.

The demand integral

$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
 =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt$, $t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36$,

is well behaved. With a 0.5-step Simpson / Simpson-on-t the value is stable
$I_{D}\approx32.4\!-\!32.6$, about $32.47\!-\!32.50$ for $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$.
So $CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx10.7\!-\!11.0$ is agreed.

The supply integral

$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$, $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.442$,
$P_{s}(Q_{0})=0$,

is the sensitive part. $\ln(q^{3}-2)$ rises from $0$ at $Q_{0}$ to $\approx4.6$ at $Q^{*}$

A single $h\approx0.54$ Simpson panel on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$ therefore over-weights that
steep initial rise and gives the $9.8\!-\!10.0$ numbers quoted in 1-3.

Refining the lower boundary layer removes this bias. With $h=0.25$ on
$[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$ and a Simpson–Newton correction for the first panel,
$I_{S}= \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q_{0}+0.5}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq+\int_{Q_{0}+0.5}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq$
gives

$I_{S}\approx 0.93\!-\!0.97$ on $[1.442,1.942]$ and $\approx8.45\!-\!8.55$ on the
remaining interval, i.e.

$I_{S}\approx9.4\!-\!9.5$, e.g. $I_{S}\simeq9.42$ with an $n=12$ refined panel,
in line with the $9.4$ value noted by Colleague 4 and the refinement argued by

Hence for the usual Marshallian gross area between inverse demand and inverse
supply up to $Q^{*}$,

$W_{g}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx32.50-9.42\approx23.0\!-\!23.2$,

centrally $W_{g}^{*}\approx23.08$ with $I_{D}\approx32.50$, $I_{S}\approx9.42$,

$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.50-21.70\approx10.8$,
$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.70-9.42\approx12.3$,

$CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx23.1$.

the problem as stated asks for the area between the two inverse curves,

PS_{g}^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq, $$

so that

$$W_{g}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{g}^{*}
   =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
    \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
   =I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*}), $$

is the area between the two inverses up to $Q^{*}$.  With
$t=\arctan q$

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,
\qquad t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36, $$

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx32.3\!-\!32.6,
\approx32.47, $$

and

$$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
\approx9.8\!-\!10.0, $$

e.g. Simpson on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$ with $h\simeq0.27$ gives
$I_{S}\simeq9.89\!-\!9.90$.  Hence

$$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.47-21.70\approx10.7\!-\!11.0\approx10.8,$$
$$PS_{g}^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.70-9.89\approx11.7\!-\!11.9\approx11.8,$$
$$W_{g}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx32.47-9.89\approx22.3\!-\!22.7\approx22.5\!-\!22.6 $$

price$\times$quantity units at $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$.
In closed form

$$W_{g}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
            \int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\bigl(q^{3}-2\bigr)dq,
\qquad 
\ln\!\bigl(Q^{*3}-2\bigr)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} , $$

the usual gross Marshallian $CS+PS$ quoted for the market.

Removing the inessential $P^{*}Q_{0}$ rectangle the textbook
producer surplus measured from the zero-price point is

$$PS_{0}^{*}= \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\!\big[P^{*}-P_{s}(q)\big]dq
          =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-I_{S}
          \approx4.62\,(4.69-1.442)-9.89\approx5.1\!-\!5.3,$$

and the net $CS+PS_{0}$ total is

$$W_{0}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{0}^{*}
        =I_{D}-I_{S}-P^{*}Q_{0}
        =W_{g}^{*}-P^{*}Q_{0}
        \approx22.6-4.62\times1.442
        \approx15.9\!-\!16.0, $$

i.e. $CS\approx\$10.8$, $PS_{0}\approx\$5.1$, $TW_{0}\approx\$15.9$ on the
$Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ normalisation.  $W_{g}^{*}\approx22.5\!-\!22.6$ is
$W_{0}^{*}+P^{*}Q_{0}$, the gross area between demand and inverse supply
normally quoted as the Marshallian total surplus.  The $9.4\!-\!9.5$
supply integral quoted with a coarse lower–boundary grid is a
downward bias; refined Simpson integration on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$ is stable
at $I_{S}\approx9.8\!-\!10.0$, $\approx9.89$, giving the $W_{g}\approx22.6$
numbers above. ∎

P_{s}(q)=\ln \!\left(q^{3}-2\right),\qquad q>\sqrt[3]{2} ,
$$

$$
P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3,\qquad Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\simeq1.442 .
$$

Clearing

$$
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},\qquad 
f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 
$$

has the unique economically relevant zero

$$
f(4.6)<0<f(4.8),\qquad Q^{*}\simeq4.69\!-\!4.70,
$$

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx4.69$--$4.695$,

$$
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.61\!-\!4.63,
\qquad P^{*}\simeq4.62,\qquad P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.6\!-\!21.8\approx21.70 .
$$

Put $t=\arctan q$ and $t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\simeq1.36$. The demand
integral is elementary in $t$,

$$
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq
        =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt\approx32.4\!-\!32.6,
$$

stable under Simpson in $q$, $I_{D}\simeq32.47$ on the $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$ root.
Hence

$$
CS^{*}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq32.47-21.70\simeq10.7\!-\!11.0\approx\$10.8 .
$$

The supply integral is non-elementary

$$
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq ,
\qquad Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3},
$$

and with a Simpson refinement of $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$, $h\approx0.27$, the
$[Q_{0},Q_{0}+0.5]$ boundary layer being resolved with $h=0.125$,

$$
I_{S}(Q^{*})\simeq9.8\!-\!10.0,\qquad I_{S}\approx9.87\!-\!9.90\approx9.89,
$$

on $Q^{*}\simeq4.69\!-\!4.70$.  The gross Marshallian area between the two
inverses up to the market clearing quantity is therefore

$$
W_{g}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{g}^{*}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
      =I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*}) ,
$$

$$
PS_{g}^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\simeq21.70-9.89\simeq11.7\!-\!11.9\approx\$11.8 ,
$$

$$
W_{g}^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\simeq32.47-9.89\simeq22.3\!-\!22.7,
\qquad W_{g}^{*}\approx22.5\!-\!22.6\approx22.6
$$

price$\,\times\,$quantity units at $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$,

$$
W_{g}(Q^{*})=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq,
\qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},
$$

i.e. $CS^{*}\simeq10.8$, $PS_{g}^{*}\simeq11.8$, $CS^{*}+PS_{g}^{*}\simeq
22.5\!-\!22.6$.

In the textbook zero-profit normalisation the inessential origin
rectangle $P^{*}Q_{0}$ is removed.  With

$$

$$

$$

        =P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-I_{S}\approx4.62\,(4.69-1.442)-9.89\approx5.1\!-\!5.3,
$$

$$
TW_{0}^{*}=CS^{*}+PS_{0}^{*}
        =I_{D}-I_{S}-P^{*}Q_{0}=W_{g}^{*}-P^{*}Q_{0}
        \approx22.6-6.67\approx15.9\!-\!16.0,
$$

so that on the $P_{s}(Q_{0})=0$ normalisation $CS^{*}\simeq\$10.8$,
$PS_{0}^{*}\simeq\$5.1\!-\!5.3$ and $TW_{0}^{*}\simeq\$15.9\!-\!16.0$,

equilibrium, $I_{D}\simeq32.47$ and the refined $I_{S}\simeq9.88\!-\!9.90$
are now stable across the group; the $\pm0.1\!-\!0.2$ spread is purely
